Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I distract myself with something else
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette:
The event that changed everything for David happened twenty-three years ago, during a period of escalating violence in the city where he had been serving a small, tight-knit Jewish community. He was thirty-nine then, a young rabbi with a wife and two young children, and he had been warned that his congregation was a target. One evening, as he walked home from evening prayers, a group of men cornered him in an alley. One of them pressed the cold, hard muzzle of a pistol against the back of his neck. They shouted at him in a language he understood only too well, their voices raw with hatred. He was beaten, robbed, and left bleeding on the ground. What stayed with him, more than the pain of the blows, was the absolute, paralyzing certainty that he was about to die, and the feeling of that weapon’s metal against his skin. He survived, but the family fled the country within the month, resettling in a quiet American suburb where he eventually rebuilt his life and his congregation.

For years, David managed. He told himself the past was the past. But the triggers, when they began to surface, were unignorable. A sudden, unexpected touch on his shoulder from a congregant after a service would make him flinch so violently that he would knock over a chair. The sight of a long, heavy flashlight in a hardware store, or a thick wooden rolling pin in a kitchen, would send a jolt of cold dread through his chest. The worst, however, was shouting. A raised voice—even a child yelling in play, even a spirited debate during a Torah study session—would make his heart hammer and his vision narrow. In those moments, he would tell himself he deserved to suffer for what had happened, a punishing thought that felt like an old, familiar payment for his own perceived failure to have prevented the attack. To cope, he began to mentally recite the week’s parsha, or count the panes of glass in the sanctuary window, anything to distract himself from the rising panic.

These moments of being triggered also began to corrode his sense of himself. He would think, with a kind of grim certainty, that somebody else—a braver man, a stronger rabbi—would have stopped the event from happening. This belief that he was fundamentally inadequate hardened into a deeper conviction: he could not rely on himself. His own body, he came to feel, was an enemy, reacting as if he were still in that alley even when he was safe in his own study. This feeling of betrayal by his own flesh and mind made him hypervigilant. He found it difficult to concentrate during services, his attention constantly scanning the exits and the faces in the back rows. He would choose his seat in the synagogue’s social hall based entirely on how safe and protected he felt, always with his back to a wall and a clear view of the door. The only place where the vigilance ever truly quieted was in the small, windowless storage room off his office, a space he had come to think of as his safe zone.

The perceived threat in the world around him began to feed back into his experience of the triggers. Because he was always scanning for danger, a sudden touch felt not just surprising, but confirmatory—proof that danger was everywhere. Because he could not concentrate, he missed the subtle cues of a congregant’s approach, making every unexpected encounter a shock. The constant state of threat also drove his maladaptive strategies deeper. He began to avoid emotional intimacy with his wife, Rachel, pulling away from her embraces and deflecting her concerned questions. He was certain that if she knew the depth of his fear, she would see him as the weak man he believed himself to be. This avoidance, in turn, only reinforced his negative appraisals. Each time he withdrew from her, he silently proved to himself that he was broken, that he could not rely on himself to be a proper husband. The punishing thoughts grew louder. The cycle tightened.

What finally brought David to seek help was a single, small incident. A young man in his congregation, trying to get his attention during a noisy Kiddush, placed a hand on his back and shouted his name over the din. David spun around, his face pale, his hands shaking, and shouted back, “Don’t touch me!” The room fell silent. He saw the hurt and confusion in the young man’s face, and the pity in the eyes of his board members. That night, Rachel told him, quietly, that she could not live like this anymore—not with his distance, not with his fear. He is now sitting in a therapist’s office, terrified that he is beyond help, but more terrified of losing the life he has spent twenty-three years trying to hold together. He is most afraid of what he might discover about himself if he looks too closely at the past.
